title: Optimise the clicks
hook: Clicks reward good articles. Chase the most clicks, and what do your readers get?

knows: what a metric is (a number used to judge something)
doesNotKnow: that optimising a proxy can drive the real goal to zero

misconception: If a metric tracks quality, pushing the metric up pushes quality up.
objective: The learner can explain that a proxy which partly rewards the real goal can still be maximised by abandoning the goal, because an optimiser takes the cheapest route to the number.

claims.text: The toy's formula is invented: an article has 10 units of effort split between hype h and substance s; clicks = 2h + s and reader value = s. The article starts at 2 hype, 8 substance (12 clicks, value 8).
claims.source: The lesson's own model in Demo.tsx (EFFORT, START_HYPE, clicks(), value()).

claims.text: With h + s = 10, clicks = h + 10, so each unit moved from substance to hype gains one click and loses one unit of value; clicks are highest at h = 10: 20 clicks, reader value 0.
claims.source: Substitute s = 10 − h. Reproduced by running runToEnd(2, "clicks") from Demo.tsx: h = 10, clicks 20, value 0.

claims.text: The optimiser moves one unit of effort per step in whichever direction raises its target; aimed at value it ends at 10 value and 10 clicks.
claims.source: step() and runToEnd() in Demo.tsx; runToEnd(2, "value") = 0, clicks(0) = 10, value(0) = 10.

claims.text: The pattern is known as Goodhart's law, often stated as “when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure”.
claims.source: The wording is Strathern 1997, “‘Improving ratings’: audit in the British University system”, European Review 5(3), 305–321, paraphrasing Goodhart 1975, “Problems of Monetary Management: the U.K. Experience”; variants classified in Manheim & Garrabrant 2018, “Categorizing Variants of Goodhart's Law”, arXiv:1803.04585.

claims.text: In this toy, substance earns one click per unit and hype earns two, so each step from substance to hype gains a click and costs a unit of reader value; a measure can stop tracking its goal once something optimises it.
claims.source: Reveal paragraphs 1-2. In the toy clicks = 2h + s rewards s by one click per unit, true. But with effort fixed at 10, clicks = h + 10 = 20 - s, so across all splits clicks and value are perfectly negatively correlated (r = -1, fact-checker script cv.mjs): the toy never shows clicks tracking value before optimisation. The first half is true of the formula; the second half is general Goodhart-style reasoning supported by c4. Added by fact-checker 2026-10-13; needs an independent check. DISPUTED 2026-10-13: The reveal says clicks and value 'look related' and that the measure 'tracks the goal' before optimisation. In the toy (effort fixed at 10) clicks = 20 - value, perfectly inverse, and the stage bars move in opposite directions; the toy never shows clicks tracking value. Fix: state the Goodhart point without claiming the toy's clicks track value, or let the toy vary total effort. | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13: Was 'clicks and value look related ... a measure that tracks the goal ... can stop tracking it' (disputed: with effort fixed, clicks = 20 - value, so the toy never shows them tracking). Dropped the 'look related' claim from the reveal. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Rechecked: clicks gain +1 and value -1 per unit moved to hype (2h+s); revised reveal no longer claims clicks track value; the Goodhart sentence is hedged ('can stop tracking').

recall.question: A support team is rewarded for closing tickets fast. Ticket closing time drops sharply. What should you check?
options: Whether customers' problems are actually being solved
Nothing: faster closing means better support
recall.why: Closing time was a proxy for good support. Once it is the target, the cheapest way to improve it, like closing unsolved tickets, can push the real goal down.
